cur:manuscripts-egberti-calming-storm.summary: In a boat with a beast-headed prow riding the waves, Christ appears twice: asleep at the stern beside the anxious apostles, and awake at the prow, raising his hand to rebuke the wind and sea. A small wind-spirit blows from the upper corner.
facts: The Codex Egberti, a Gospel lectionary made for Archbishop Egbert of Trier, is described as the oldest surviving New Testament picture cycle of the life of Christ in the Ottonian era: 52 of its 60 paintings illustrate Gospel readings in the order of the church year.
During the Second World War the codex was evacuated to Giessen University Library, survived its bombing in December 1944, and was brought back to Trier in May 1945 from a parsonage at Elkerhausen.

cur:monumental-santo-stefano-rotondo-cro.summary: In the small apse, a tall jewelled cross rises from a flowered meadow between the martyrs Primus and Felician, who stand in white and gold against the gold ground; above the cross a small medallion holds the bust of Christ. Cross and portrait together express the identity of the crucified and the glorified Lord.
facts: The chapel was built in 648 by Pope Theodore I, who brought there the relics of the martyrs Primus and Felician and buried his father in it.
The cross with a medallion of Christ above it echoes the cross with Christ's portrait in the apse of Sant'Apollinare in Classe, Ravenna.

cur:monumental-santo-stefano-rotondo-cro.notes: The Commons file description dates the mosaic 'ca. 523–530', which conflicts with the chapel's foundation by Theodore I (642–649) given by Wikipedia; the later date is followed here.

cur:monumental-mustair-flight-into-egypt.summary: The Virgin rides a donkey holding the haloed Christ Child, led by a figure in front, while Joseph, haloed and carrying a bundle, follows at the right; a city gate frames the scene. The brisk outlines and lively movement are typical of the Müstair painters.
facts: The abbey of Saint John at Müstair, founded c. 780, preserves wall paintings of about 800 arranged in five registers: the life of David at the top, three rows on the youth, ministry and Passion of Christ, and below them scenes of Saint Andrew, joined on the west wall by a Last Judgment.
UNESCO, which inscribed the abbey in 1983, describes them as Switzerland's greatest series of figurative murals, painted around 800.

Q116410370.summary: A Byzantine ivory of the Crucifixion is set like a jewel at the heart of a gilded-silver book cover studded with sapphire, glass and rock crystal. Christ hangs upright on the cross with arms outstretched, the Virgin and Saint John stand on either side, and two half-length angels hover above. Carved in Constantinople in the tenth century and remounted in Spain about a century later, the cover shows how prized Byzantine images of the Passion were in the medieval West.
facts: The Met notes that the ivory originally formed the centre of a Byzantine three-panelled icon before being reused in this binding.
The cover may have been one of the many gifts to the nunnery of Santa Cruz de la Serós, founded by Queen Felicia (d. 1085), wife of Sancho V Ramírez of Aragon and Navarre.
A sapphire seal set to the right of Saint John is inscribed in Arabic with four of the ninety-nine 'Beautiful Names' of God.
Q116410370.notes: Met accession 17.190.134 (Gift of J. Pierpont Morgan, 1917). Also published by the Met as 'Book Cover with Byzantine Icon of the Crucifixion'.

walters:W.432.60R.summary: Christ kneels in prayer on a grassy slope before a rocky outcrop, his hands raised, while Peter, James and John sleep in the foreground, one with a sword. At the left, beyond a wattle fence and gate, the crowd led by Judas is already approaching. The miniature heads the Passion according to John, whose opening words, 'Egressus est Dominus Iesus cum discipulis suis trans torrentem Cedron', begin beside it.
facts: This small miniature (11 lines high) begins the Passion narrative from John 18 in an early 16th-century prayer book from Leiden.
The Walters describes the book as notable for its abundance of illumination, with nearly sixty small miniatures; the Gospel images are largely in grisaille, though this one is fully coloured.
The manuscript belonged to Edwin H. Lawrence and W. C. Hazlitt in London and to Marshall C. Lefferts in New York before Henry Walters acquired it.

walters:W.432.60R.notes: Origin in Leiden and the date 1500–1525 follow the Walters manuscript description (TEI, The Digital Walters). The worklist year (800) was a parsing error for '1st quarter 16th century'.
